articles.title: Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
articles.summary: Pitching wins championships.
articles.body:
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.

Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.

Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?

ATL | BOS | CHC | CLE | CWS | HOU | LAD | MIL | NYY | PHI | SD | TB | TEX

RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP) RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP) RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP) RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)

The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.

Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.

With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.

RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP) RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP) RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP) LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin

The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.

Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.

Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.

LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP) RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP) LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP) LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad

The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.

Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.

Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.

B/R's Undisputed MLB Outfielder Rankings 🔢

RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP) RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP) RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP) LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez

The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.

Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.

Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.

RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP) LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP) RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP) LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)

Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.

Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.

The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.

LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP) RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP) RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP) RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)

Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.

Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.

Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.

RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP) RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP) LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP) RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)

Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan

Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.

Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.

Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.

RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP) LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP) LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP) RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)

Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval

Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.

Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.

The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.

RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP) RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP) RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP) RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)

Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)

Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.

That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.

They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.

LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP) RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP) RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP) LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)

Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.

Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).

The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.

RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP) LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP) RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP) LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)

With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.

Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.

It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.

RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP) LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP) LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP) RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)

Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan , LHP Justin Wrobleski

The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.

The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.

Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

articles.title: Trump administration considers building baseball park in Grand Teton National Park
articles.summary: Major League Baseball contacted the administration about hosting a game in a national park, with an agency official scouting Grand Teton as a possible locati...
articles.body:
Major League Baseball has approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at a national park, officials from the White House and MLB confirmed Saturday.

The administration has scouted locations in Grand Teton National Park to build a baseball park to host an MLB game, according to two other people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Grand Teton is the country's eighth-most-visited national park and is famous for its breathtaking views of the Teton Range of the Rocky Mountains. National parks are among the country's most protected federal lands, and constructing a sports facility at Grand Teton could set a new precedent for the use of vast national park land in the Western United States.

News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

An MLB official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said the league approached the administration after the success of MLB's other stand-alone events, such as the recurring Field of Dreams game in Iowa. The idea of playing a game in a national park is one of several that MLB is exploring.

The White House said in a statement that MLB asked the administration "if it was possible to host a game at a national park, similar to the Field of Dreams game."

"This is not a Presidential directive, nor is it being directed by the White House. It's also not being driven by the Department of Interior," the statement said. "Therefore, this is not a White House or Administration priority."

The White House said MLB has not made any decisions and the Park Service has not granted any permits. "If the MLB wants to go on site visits of national parks, that is their prerogative," the statement said.

It referred additional questions to MLB.

National Park Service Deputy Director Frank Lands visited Grand Teton National Park in recent days and looked at three potential locations for a baseball park within the park's boundaries, the two people familiar with the matter said.

One of the sites that Lands visited is already disturbed land that is not pristine park property, these individuals said. Many parks have "bone yards" or storage areas for materials or equipment not being used.

Lands, reached by phone Saturday evening, declined to comment.

After publication of this piece, the White House said in a statement that Lands "has not been actively scouting sites" and was on an official trip to several national parks including Grand Teton, Yellowstone and Grand Canyon.

"The MLB happened to schedule their trip to Grand Teton at the same time that Frank was there," it said. "It is incorrect to say that Frank is actively scouting sites. It is also incorrect to say that the administration is sending officials to scout sites."

A prized national park like Grand Teton is not an appropriate place for a baseball park, said Betsy Buffington, Northern Rockies regional director for the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy group.

"It is irreplaceable. There is no other Grand Teton that is home to bears and wolves and bison, elk and pronghorn," Buffington said in an interview. "So the idea that we would put a baseball stadium in Grand Teton National Park is just — what would the word be? — ludicrous. Crazy. Ridiculous. I mean, I just can't fathom."

Luther Propst, a county commissioner for Teton County, Wyoming, who met Lands this week on his visit there, said in an interview that the federal government had not sought county input and that Lands did not mention the issue.

"Grand Teton National Park is about wild America, wildlife, opportunity for solitude, not for more amusement," Propst said, calling the proposal for a ballpark "a radical departure from the tradition of national parks. "

Since assuming office in January 2025, President Donald Trump has taken actions to drastically reshape the National Park Service. His efforts to shrink the government resulted in the Park Service losing a quarter of its staff, which has at times led to closures of some park facilities , fewer tours at national parks and other disruptions. The president has sought to scrub the Park Service of signs and information related to historic racism, gender discrimination and Indigenous persecution.

The administration is also weighing whether to give a sliver of Yosemite National Park to a private developer to build road access to a resort in exchange for land of equal value. Park advocates say that giving up park land for goals other than conservation sets a new and dangerous precedent.

Starting in 2016, MLB has staged single games at various locations across the country: once at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina; once in Omaha, tied to the College World Series; once at the historic Negro League ballpark, Rickwood Field, in Birmingham; once at Bristol Motor Speedway, a NASCAR racetrack in Bristol, Tennessee; three times in Dyersville, Iowa, in the cornfield made famous by the movie "Field of Dreams"; and annually at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, tied to the Little League World Series.

Most of those were played at permanent facilities, but after the Bristol game, racetrack officials disassembled the stadium and donated some of the materials.

The Field of Dreams stadium was initially temporary, but the site was eventually expanded to make it permanent.

The 2027 MLB schedule is set and includes a Field of Dreams game and a Little League Classic game, so no new specialty game can take place before 2028.

images.caption: FILE - The Teton mountains reflect on Oxbow Bend in Grand Teton National Park in Moran, Wyo., on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. (AP Photo/Amber Baesler, File)

articles.title: Dodgers reach 100 wins in final game of regular season, setting record for manager Dave Roberts
articles.summary: The Dodgers have either won 100 games or the National League in every season since 2017.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers finished off the 2026 MLB regular season by entering 100-win territory, making history for manager Dave Roberts in the process.

With a 5-1 extra-innings win over the San Francisco Giants , the Dodgers improved their record to 100-62, winning the NL West by nine games. It is the first time they've won 100 games since the 2023 season and the 12th time in franchise history.

It is also the Dodgers' sixth 100-win season under manager Dave Roberts, tying him with Joe McCarthy and Bobby Cox for the most by a manager in MLB history. Roberts was previously tied for third at five with Connie Mack and Earl Weaver.

Every manager in the previous two sentences is a Hall of Famer, except for Roberts.

Sunday's win saw both teams employ a bullpen game, resulting in a 1-1 tie after nine innings. The Dodgers poured things on in the 10th inning, capped off by a three-run homer from center fielder Andy Pages .

Roberts' previous 100-win seasons were in 2017, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2023. The club has either won 100 games or the National League in every season following Roberts' first year in the dugout in 2016.

Roberts, of course, has benefited from being the manager of an organization that possesses both MLB's deepest pockets and one of the best front offices in baseball. He was specifically brought in to act as a conduit between the roster and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman's offices, a job he has capably performed for more than a decade now.

That's not something just anyone can do. Roberts has had to sell reduced playing time to both veterans and younger players and maintain clubhouse harmony despite championship expectations every season. He might make tactical errors at times, not to mention controversial decisions, but there's a reason he's still here despite often coming up short of a title before Shohei Ohtani came along.

The Dodgers now enter the postseason looking for the first World Series threepeat since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees . They received a bye with the second-best record in the NL, behind the 103-59 Milwaukee Brewers, and will face the winner of the wild-card series between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies in the NLDS next weekend.

images.caption: Dave Roberts has seen plenty of success with the Dodgers. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

articles.title: MLB wild-card preview: Series predictions, X-factors and more for Red Sox-Yankees, Cubs-Padres, Phillies-Braves and White Sox-Astros
articles.summary: The best time of the baseball year is finally here. Here's what you need to know for the wild-card round.
articles.body:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap .

Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.

Game 1: Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL) Game 2: Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL) Game 3: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)

Phillies : It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in the month of September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.

Braves : It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.

Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón , Mike Yazstremski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley .

Ronald Acuña Jr. , that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.

The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.

Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.

Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.

Phillies : Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sanchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not at all outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.

Braves : It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.

But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees ) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.

Game 1: David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU) Game 2: Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU) Game 3: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)

White Sox : The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. It was the offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami , that was the driving force behind the Sox's success, and they finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.

The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.

Astros : For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past . Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday .

Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?

Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.

Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.

Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.

That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.

White Sox : The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.

Astros : Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz . Perhaps Jose Altuve , 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.

No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees

Game 1: Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY) Game 2: Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY) Game 3: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)

Red Sox : Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet , made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.

Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.

The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.

Yankees : For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe , Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.

And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.

The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge . The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.

It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.

So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.

García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.

For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.

Red Sox : Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.

Yankees : No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt , trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.

Game 1: Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD) Game 2: Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD) Game 3: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)

Cubs : It was Pete Crow-Armstrong 's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.

Alex Bregman 's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.

But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.

Padres : San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals , Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.

Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.

Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24

San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr . turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller , Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.

Cubs : Alex Bregman — specifically, his face

One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle . Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.

There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.

Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.

This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?

Cubs : The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.

Padres : The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

articles.title: Joe Espada's future is uncertain, but AL West title is a time to celebrate. 'He kept everyone cool'
articles.summary: Manager Joe Espada was the constant in an Astros season that ended in AL West title after team overcame injuries and adversity.
articles.body:
WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. - Amid a simmering celebration ready to erupt, Joe Espada called for silence. About him milled Houston Astros players wearing ski goggles and division champion T-shirts. Against the sound of corks popping, Espada embarked on a short speech.

"Early in the season, adversity came in hard on us - very hard," Espada began. "Mid-May, we were down in the standings, down in our record, 10, 15 games under 500. When adversity came knocking at that door, you guys never opened that door. You guys just came together and came closer together, 'cause you guys knew that at the end of the day, you were the best team in the West …"

Shortly before, the Astros had reclaimed that distinction. Houston on Sunday won its eighth American League West title in 10 years. This one resembled none of those before it. The Astros finished 81-81 to claim a division in which no other team finished above .500 or posted a positive run differential.

These Astros are the first MLB team to reach the postseason with a non-winning record in a full-length season. Just six other teams since at least 1900 have started 20-31, as they did, or worse and made the playoffs, per Baseball Reference.

In another season - or another division this season - that start might have buried them. Avoiding it still required a measure of resilience. To what extent that emanates from a manager is debatable, as it's the players who must produce. Yet results also reflect on those at the helm.

"You need a voice of reason," said first baseman Christian Walker . "You need that slow and steady. One hundred sixty-two (games) over six, seven months, it's a crazy thing. It's a marathon for sure. I think he (Espada) does a great job of letting us run our clubhouse and control the culture and just making sure he holds us accountable."

This is the third season as manager for Espada, who spent six previous years as the Astros' bench coach. It featured some parallels to his first. In 2024, the Astros started 7-19, the second-worst record to that point of a season in franchise history. They were 10 games out of first place on June 18. They wound up with 88 wins and a division title, before losing to the Detroit Tigers in the wild-card round.

Espada's constant positivity and patience garnered some recognition after that turnaround. Last season yielded a different kind, as the Astros squandered a seven-game division lead at midseason and missed the playoffs. Team officials cited injuries as a factor, but the end of the franchise's streak of eight straight playoff appearances, while fielding a top-10 payroll, did not sit well.

Ineffectiveness and injuries hit the Astros hard again early this season. Sixteen players resided on their injured list in late April, including shortstop Jeremy Peña , ace Hunter Brown and closer Josh Hader . Third baseman Carlos Correa suffered a season-ending ankle injury in early May. On May 20, the Astros fell to 20-31 and a season-high-tying six games out of first place, with the worst team ERA in the majors.

Going 61-50 the rest of the way - the fourth-highest winning percentage in the AL in that span after the Red Sox , Rays and Yankees - proved enough to make them a playoff team. Espada credited his players with creating that pivot. In all, he used 19 different starting pitchers, a franchise record. Sixteen players made at least one start in his outfield - 12 in left field alone - and 10 in the cleanup spot.

"Any other team would have folded, but these guys chose not to, man," Espada said Sunday afternoon. "It's about the character of this team. They just don't quit, and they fight, they stay together."

Making the postseason is a mandate for Houston. Astros owner Jim Crane made that clear in August, after he dismissed general manager Dana Brown in the middle of a playoff race.

Brown was in his final year under contract. So is Espada. Crane, a day after dismissing Brown, affirmed that Espada would at least finish the season as manager - remarking that "Joe's doing what he can do with what he's got" - but deferred a decision on Espada's future to after the season.

The Astros, at least, delayed that consideration further with their return to the playoffs. They will host the Chicago White Sox in a best-of-three wild-card series beginning Tuesday at Daikin Park, securing a spot on the final day of a season in which they never climbed more than four games above .500.

"Joe was great for us all year," Peña said. "He kept us level-headed. We had a lot of things that didn't go the way we wanted from the jump. But I feel like Joe, as the head of the group, as the leader, he kept everyone cool, calm and collected, and we got into the postseason."

With that official, the Astros encircled Espada in the visitors' batting cage at Sutter Health Park. Espada started by recognizing Yordan Alvarez , the slugger who claimed a batting title and carried the Astros' offense all season, bringing him into the center and wrapping a wrestling-style belt, similar to the ones the Astros present their hitter and pitcher of the game after wins, around Alvarez's waist.

"In my f- book, you're the heavyweight champion of the world," Espada told Alvarez.

The Astros cheered. Espada asked Alvarez if he'd like to address them. Alvarez demurred, and Espada began the short speech to his team that he concluded as such:

"I am so proud of all you guys, man. Young players, veteran players, training staff keeping these guys on the field, coaching staff, I am so proud of you guys. Hey, we won the West. Let's go."

His final words drowned in a din of shouts and sparkling spray, as the Astros feted an aspiration fulfilled.

"It's a team that's been there before, and that matters," Espada said afterward. "We're going to be in front of our home crowd, that matters too. In '24, that wild-card (series), we didn't play our best. And we'll be better. Just looking forward to it, man."
