articles.title: 2026 Dbacks Prospects All Stars: Starting Battery & Infield Corners
articles.summary: A look at the best starting pitcher, catcher(s), and firstbaseman and thirdbaseman in the Dbacks farm system in 2026
articles.body:
With the regular season now over for both Major League and Minor League Baseball, I think now would a be good time take a look at the best individual performance at each position in the Diamondbacks farm system. For the sake of the reader and my own sanity, we're going to look at just the starting battery and infield corner positions today, otherwise this would be a very long read.

Before I do that, I want to congratulate the D'Backs Double-A affiliate, the Amarillo Sod Poodles, on winning the Texas League Championship. Winning a championship is great for the development of the younger players on the team, especially those who might not have had the best individual season this year. That said, about half the players mentioned in the next few articles will be players on that team.

David Hagaman is the clear and obvious answer for the best starting pitcher in the Diamondbacks farm system in 2026, and the pitcher most likely to actually be named the Dbacks MILB pitcher of the year. There really isn't much competition, especially knowing the context behind the numbers.

Hagaman, who was acquired in last summer's Merrill Kelly trade, started the year assigned to high-A Hillsboro in the pitcher friendly confines of the Northwestern League. Across 15 games, Hagaman put up 71⅓ innings with a 3.03 ERA, 4.10 FIP, and 4.15 xFIP. Adjusted for the League that works out to a very impressive 61 ERA- and a slightly less impressive 84 FIP-. His 10.85 strikeouts per nine innings and 28% strikeout percentage are very impressive as well. That alone might not be enough to make him pitcher of the year, but what he did after being promoted to Double-A Amarillo, in the much more hitter friendly Texas League that cemented him as the organization's pitcher of the year.

Hagaman started seven games, putting up 35 ⅓ innings with a 2.55 ERA, a 3.22 FIP, and a 3.79 xFIP. His strikeout percentage went up to 32.4% and 11.72 strikeouts per nine innings. He also walked less batters, going from 10.7% to 8.5%. In the hitter friendly Texas league, that translates to a 43 ERA- and a 75 ERA-. Hagaman did struggle with walks though in his post season outing in the Texas League division series and the championship to a lesser extent. It'll be interesting to see if he returns to Double-A next season, gets promoted to Triple-A Reno, or possibly even has a chance at making his MLB debut with a strong showing in spring training. My first article going in depth on Dbacks pitching prospects has a scouting report if you're interested in reading more about him, which you can read here .

Gabriel Moreno has won the NL batting title, which I'm pointing out now because it really helps show just how strong the Diamondbacks organization is right now at the catching position from top to bottom, and how many of them had very good seasons this year, which is how this turned into another multi part series.

The Dbacks reinforced that position of strength after using their first round pick on a well regarded college catcher, Ryder Helfrick, who went on to have a solid professional debut in the Low A level California League. Despite putting up a solid triple slash line of .245/.327/.521 with a 104 wRC+ in just 24 games, that's just 24 games, so he's not the All Star here.

Jhosep Villarroel put up eye popping numbers in his 47 games this summer, but he's also a 17 year old in the Dominican Summmer League, so you have to take these number with a massive grain of salt, which is why he's not my All-Star but another honorable mention. That said his numbers are REALLY good, it's just a small sample size and he's very young. Combined between the two Dbacks DSL teams he hit .303/.500/.485 with a .493 wOBA and a 148 OPS+. Villarroel will almost certainly make his stateside debut with either the ACL Dbacks or Visalia Rawhide next season, which will give us a much better chance to evaluate him as a prospect.

It's also not Alberto Barriga , who tore up the pitcher friendly Northwestern League for 40 games, hitting 259/.345/.490 with a 113 wRC+. The reason he's not is that he struggled in the extremely hitter friendly Texas League after being being promoted, hittng just 237/301/362 with .302 wOBA and 55 wRC+ in 57 Games. He's one of the players mentioned in the intro who I think will benefit a lot from the experience gained in Amarillo's championship run. Barriga's probably the most unique of the catching prospects here, so I am really looking forward to seeing how he adjust next season.

Ivan Luciano has a very solid argument based on his above average play in 2026. Luciano spent the majority (85 games) of the season in Visalia, where he hit 264/.375/.441 with .372 wOBA and a 109 wRC+. In the 12 games in Hillsboro after being promoted, he hit .279/.380/.465 with a .383 wOBA and 122 WRC+. Combined across the two levels, Luciano put up a solidly above average tripleslash of .266/.376/.444 with a .374 wOBA and 111 wRC+. One of his teammates (at the beginning of the season) has a much stronger argument based on his numbers, and that's Carlos Virahonda.

Carlos Virahonda started the year with 48 games in Visalia in which he hit .273/.359 /.508 .383 wOBA and 115 wRC+. He was then promoted to High A Hillsboro and in 50 games, and a in much more pitcher friendly league, where he'd hit .272/.393/.468 with a .391 wOBA and a 127 wRC+. He'd then finish his season playing in four games with Double A Amarillo, where he'd go 4 for 15 with a pair of doubles and a homerun, while getting plunked three times to give him a .267/.389/.600 and a 134 wC+. In 108 games combined across all three levels, Virahonda hit .272/.377/.493 with 18 HRS, a .388 wOBA and a 122 wRC+. To cap it all off, he also had a fantastic post season with Amarillo, playing a key role offensively.

If you'd like to read a more in depth look at the catchers, check out this article from earlier this season.

Danny Serretti could have easily been an all-star at second base, but he had slightly more innings as a third baseman. There also really aren't any other obvious candidates at the position, unlike second base which is just as stacked as catcher, so we're sticking Serretti here. I had an article focused on Serretti's background prior to this season, which you can read here if you are so interested.

Serreti spent a lot of time going back and forth between Amarillo and Reno, even coming back to play a key role in Amarillo's championship. In 74 games in Amarillo he hit 272/.418/.510 with a .413 wOBA and a 124 WRC+. In 35 games in Reno, he hit .316/.421/.513 with a .419 wOBA a .357 xWOBA, and a 129 wRC+. His walk percentage fell slightly from 17.8% to 14.9%, but I'd attribute that to the higher batting average, which is backed up by his strikeout percentage staying within .3% of each other, with Serretti striking out 22.4% in Amarillo and 22.7% in Reno. As a whole, Serretti finished his season hitting 287/419/.511 with 19 homeruns, 11 stolen bases, a .415 wOBA and a 126 wRC+ in 109 games.

The only other third baseman in the same ballpark (at times literally) was LuJames Groover, who was above average in Reno but struggled at the MLB level in 2026.

Finally, at least for this week, we have another position with a single clear and obvious choice.

Manuel Pena broke out in a big way in 2026, hitting 26 homeruns in 61 games with Amarillo, while also putting up a triple slash line of .311/354/.673 with a robust .428 wOBA and 134 wRC+ in the first half of the season . After being promoted to Reno he'd cool down significantly, but overall in 112 games he would hit .305/.345/.555 with a 108 wRC+ with 31 HRs. The only other first baseman who had better numbers in the Dbacks farm system were Pavin Smith and Tyler Locklear and I don't think anyone reading this wants to hear more about either player.

That's it for now! Next time, I'll look at the middle infield and outfielders.

articles.title: MLB Playoffs 2026 Wild Card and Round-by-Round Bracket Picks and Predictions
articles.summary: Ask yourself now: are you ready?
articles.body:
Ready or not, the MLB postseason will begin Tuesday with the NLWCS and ALWCS. Given the labor uncertainty in the sport, it's important to savor this final month of baseball.

With that in mind, let's get to full predictions for the 2026 MLB postseason, starting with the Wild Card Series and going all the way to selecting a World Series champion.

AL Wild Card Series A: No. 5 Boston Red Sox at No. 4 New York Yankees

Schedule: 8 p.m. ET on NBC and Peacock Tuesday-Thursday

Regular-Season Series: Yankees 7, Red Sox 6

Matchup to Watch: Aroldis Chapman vs. Yankees

Aroldis Chapman spent parts of seven seasons across two stints with the Yankees, recording 153 saves, the most of any team in his likely Cooperstown-bound career. But it's fair to say things didn't end well in the Bronx, with Chapman saying earlier this year that he thinks Brian Cashman owes him an apology.

So it would be quite a turn of events if Chapman—still one of the league's most dominant relievers at 38—had the chance to end the Yankees' season in New York.

When Yankees manager Aaron Boone was asked Sunday—via Greg Joyce of The New York Post—what Aaron Judge (right calf strain) is doing with the postseason looming, he said, "not a whole lot yet."

It goes without saying that the three-time AL MVP's availability and effectiveness, if he can play, will go a long way toward determining the outcome of this series.

Prediction: Red Sox over Yankees in three

The Yankees and Red Sox will split Games 1 and 2 before Ranger Suárez—the pitcher with a 1.48 career postseason ERA—turns in a dominant outing in Game 3 to give Boston a series win.

AL Wild Card Series B: No. 6 Chicago White Sox at No. 3 Houston Astros

Schedule: 5 p.m. ET on Peacock and NBC Sports Network Tuesday-Thursday

Regular-Season Series: Astros 5, White Sox 2

Matchup to Watch : Munetaka Murakami vs. Astros

Munetaka Murakami hit .232 with 20 homers and a .911 OPS in the first half. After the All-Star Break, he hit .184 with 15 homers and a .750 OPS. If the White Sox can get Murakami to rediscover his first-half form, they won't just win this series; they could go pretty far in a wide-open AL.

X-Factor: The greatness of Yordan Alvarez

In a series this short, if one superstar gets hot, that can be all it takes to win. Alvarez is the likely AL MVP and has a .944 OPS in 60 career postseason games. The White Sox absolutely cannot let the former ALCS MVP beat them.

As great as Alvarez is, the Astros are one of the worst regular-season teams ever to reach the postseason, winning a weak AL West at 81-81. We'll give them a game at home, but this series will be about the national emergence of Miguel Vargas, one of the best players in baseball this season, who could wear out the Crawford boxes.

NL Wild Card Series A: No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies at No. 3 Atlanta Braves

Schedule: 2 p.m. ET on NBC and Peacock Tuesday-Thursday

Regular-Season Series: Braves 9, Phillies 4

Matchup to Watch: Bryce Harper vs. Braves

While Ronald Acuña Jr. loves to play the heel at Citizens Bank Park, Bryce Harper does at Truist Park as well. A weekend after Acuña did quite a bit of celebrating at Citizens Bank Park earlier this September, Harper returned the favor with a slow home run trot in Atlanta:

Harper has been around long enough to have played at Turner Field. Since Truist Park opened in 2017, he's got 18 home runs and a .916 OPS in road games against the Braves.

For the Phillies to upset the Braves, they'll likely need a big series from the two-time NL MVP.

The Braves won the NL East in both 2022 and 2023, but the Phillies upset them in the NLDS in back-to-back seasons. Granted, that came after a first-round bye, but both teams have much of their core in place. If the Braves get down early in Game 1, will they start to feel like here we going again ?

The Phillies have had the Braves number in the postseason in this era, but before winning on the final day of the season to clinch a playoff spot, they looked on the verge of collapsing. Chris Sale (3-0, 2.48 ERA in four starts) and Tyler Mahle (1-1, 2.48 ERA in four starts) both pitched well against the Phillies this season and expect that to continue. With Zack Wheeler needing to be used the final day of the regular season and Jesús Luzardo's status uncertain, the Braves will beat the Phillies.

NL Wild Card Series B: No. 5 Chicago Cubs at No. 4 San Diego Padres

Schedule: 10 p.m. ET on Peacock and NBCSN

Matchup to Watch: Pete Crow-Armstrong vs. Padres pitching

Pete Crow-Armstrong is the likely NL MVP. The Cubs don't have great starting pitching, but between PCA, Alex Bregman and Seiya Suzuki, they have the bats to outhit some of their pitching concerns. Slowing down Crow-Armstrong is probably easier said than done, but he homered four times and drove in 10 runs in six games against the Friars this year. If he hits anything like that, the Padres will be heading home.

For as imposing as the Cubs' offensive stars can be, the Padres have by far the best bullpen in baseball. If Craig Stammen's club has the lead after six innings, there's a pretty good chance that a group led by Mason Miller, Adrián Morejón, Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam and Yuki Matsui won't be giving up the league.

Fernando Tatis Jr. and the Padres have been baseball's best team in September, but there's been a magic with the Cubs in 2026. Alex Bregman looked good to go Sunday, and his playoff experience will help guide the Cubs to a road-series victory despite a shaky bullpen.

ALDS 1: Cleveland Guardians over White Sox

The White Sox's magical run— two seasons after losing 121 games—will end at the hands of the Cleveland Guardians, the team that swiped the division from under them in September.

Cleveland is back in the postseason for the third time in as many years under Stephen Vogt. It is concerning that José Ramírez hit just .195 in September, but Steven Kwan rediscovered his stroke after the All-Star Break, hitting .353 with an .875 OPS following the Midsummer Classic. With Kwan and excellent pitching, the Guardians will advance to the ALCS for the second time in three years. Guardians in four .

The three best teams in the American League this year were all in the AL East. The Red Sox were dispatched by the Yankees in the first round, but they'll face a Rays team that might be the best in franchise history.

Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda are a tremendous trio to lead your lineup, and while the Rays' approach to pitching isn't everyone's cup of tea, it works for them. We'll go Rays in four games.

It's hard to win the World Series two years in a row, which the Dodgers found out last year. Doing it three seasons in a row is nearly impossible. Even with a star-studded roster—which has added two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal since we last saw them in October—the bet here is that this is the year the Dodgers are knocked off.

History shows this is the best round to catch the Dodgers, as they were upset by the San Diego Padres in 2022 and the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2023 after a first-round bye. Granted, that was before they employed Shohei Ohtani. But Sale pitched a complete-game shutout against the Dodgers in August, and if he can set the tone early in the series, it could get late for Dave Roberts' squad fast. We'll go Braves in four .

This should be a great matchup between two NL Central rivals with World Series aspirations. Few storylines are better than Craig Counsell squaring off against his former team, led by his college coach, Pat Murphy.

Perhaps more than any other team in the postseason, the Brewers need to win Game 1. Jacob Misiorowski—who will likely win the NL Cy Young unanimously—has little margin for error this postseason, but his pitching this year suggests he can handle it.

In a best-of-five series where Misiorowski will likely start two games, the Brew Crew will probably need to win just one game started by someone other than their ace. Whether it's Logan Henderson or Shane Drohan, Milwaukee will have enough pitching to defeat the Cubs. Brewers in five .

In a couple of months, owners will lock the players out, suggesting that Major League Baseball's competitive integrity needs a salary cap. Those same owners would likely cringe at an ALCS matchup between the Guardians and Rays, teams that rank 30th and 23rd in payroll.

Granted, this is the worst American League playoff field in at least a generation, but both teams have the pitching to make a deep October run.

In Cleveland, Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Joey Cantillo are a strong rotation trio. Imagine if they can get Foster Griffin—who posted a 5.19 ERA after being acquired from the Washington Nationals—back on track. Cleveland's bullpen might not be as dominant as two years ago, but Cade Smith, Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and Tim Herrin are a quartet that's not going to blow many leads.

Unfortunately for the Guardians, the Rays have a strong starting rotation of their own. It would obviously help if Shane McClanahan made an impact at some point in the postseason, but Nick Martinez, Drew Rasmussen, Griffin Jax and a resurgent Freddy Peralta are pretty tough. Oh, and Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly were two of the best relievers in baseball this season.

Rays in six , as Tampa will win its third AL pennant in franchise history.

Five years ago, the Braves won the World Series, but did so without Acuña, who sustained a torn right ACL that August. This time around, Acuña will be in the lineup for a Braves team that wins the pennant.

It may not have been a great season for Acuña, but he hit .307 with a .950 OPS in September. At his best, he's as good as anyone in baseball. If he hits his stride, a lineup that also includes Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II will be a problem. Heck, imagine what they'll look like if either Ozzie Albies or Austin Riley shows signs of life.

That's not to take away from the Brewers, who won a franchise-record 103 games, the most in baseball this year. Brice Turang is the most underappreciated star in baseball, and between Jackson Chourio, William Contreras and Jake Bauers, there's a lot of really good here.

But for the second season in a row, we're predicting that the Brewers will fall just shy of reaching the World Series for the first time since 1982. They won't be swept this time, but they just don't have enough starting pitching after Misiorowski to sustain a deep playoff run.

Atlanta doesn't have the best rotation either, but Mahle has been a revelation since being acquired, while Grant Holmes has posted a 3.44 ERA over 151.2 innings. We're predicting that Martín Pérez returns from a back injury in this series, and the Braves win in six games .

MLB owners, hell-bent on getting a salary cap, would probably love nothing more than the Dodgers winning a third consecutive World Series title as the lead-in to a prolonged labor battle.

Instead, they'll have to figure out how to make their case after the Rays—a perennial success despite ownership not spending much—win their franchise's first World Series title. They've previously been to the Fall Classic in 2008 and 2020, but lost both.

This time, Caminero will grab the attention of even the most casual baseball fans with his prodigious power. By hitting 42 home runs, Caminero has himself in the AL MVP race. He'll probably come up short, but a World Series MVP would be a hell of a consolation prize.

The Braves may make it this far with Sale and Mahle leading their rotation, but ultimately they're a starting pitcher or two short of winding up on a parade float. Rays in six games , with Tampa clinching in their first season back at Tropicana Field.

To celebrate their World Series title, the Rays will announce they are returning to being the Devil Rays in 2027. (OK, we're trying to speak that last part into existence a bit.)

articles.title: Final MLB Power Rankings of Regular Season Before 2026 Postseason
articles.summary: Heading into the 2026 Major League Baseball season, the New York Mets, Seattle Mariners and Toronto Blue Jays looked like three of the biggest challengers to the Dodgers dynasty. Meanwhile the Tampa Bay Rays were supposed to finish in dead last in the AL East and a fourth consecutive season with at least 100 losses felt like a real possibility for the Chicago White Sox.
articles.body:
Heading into the 2026 Major League Baseball season, the New York Mets, Seattle Mariners and Toronto Blue Jays looked like three of the biggest challengers to the Dodgers dynasty. Meanwhile the Tampa Bay Rays were supposed to finish in dead last in the AL East and a fourth consecutive season with at least 100 losses felt like a real possibility for the Chicago White Sox.

Good thing they played the games instead of letting preseason predictions and win total odds decide the postseason seeding, right?

Deviating from our normal weekly tradition of comparing each team's current ranking to where we had them seven days ago, we'll be noting where each of the 30 teams appeared in our preseason power rankings .

For the 12 postseason-bound teams—who will all appear in our top 12 on principle—we'll focus on how they're looking heading into the playoffs.

For the other 18 who have already shifted into offseason mode, we'll at least find something nice to say about their regular season.

After all, for some of them, it's been a while since anyone did.

In case you missed it, B/R's MLB Power Rankings from last week and every fresh power rankings throughout the season can be found at the new MLB Power Rankings hub .

30. Colorado Rockies (58-104) Preseason Rank: 29

Colorado sure did crater to the finish line, going 8-30 from August 17 onward. But they didn't suffer 119 losses, and their run differential (minus-192) was merely pretty darn bad as opposed to historically awful (minus-424). That's an improvement upon last season. They even bested their preseason win total of 55.5. Baby steps are better than back pedaling.

29. Los Angeles Angels (62-100) Preseason Rank: 26

While Mike Trout wasn't exactly his old dominant self, he was as healthy as we've seen him in more than a decade, appearing in more than 140 games for the first time since 2016. Alongside that now 12-time All-Star, the Halos had a breakout star in rookie Walbert Ureña, posting a 2.97 ERA in 148.1 innings of work.

28. Athletics (64-98) Preseason Rank: 23

As the injuries piled up, things unraveled in a hurry for the Athletics, going 26-60 after starting 38-38. But Zack Gelof bounced back admirably from brutal 2024 and 2025 campaigns while Henry Bolte emerged as the center fielder of the future. Pair them with a healthy Nick Kurtz, Jacob Wilson, Tyler Soderstrom, Brent Rooker and Shea Langeliers and this may have been a different story. Alas.

27. San Francisco Giants (65-97) Preseason Rank: 13

Speaking of the injury bug, the Giants spent six months walking through a swarm of them, seemingly never close to full strength after Opening Day. But after a slow start, at least Rafael Devers caught fire. Over his final 112 games, he hit 35 home runs while posting a .959 OPS. That would've been the best mark of his career were it not for that .570 OPS through the first 36 contests.

26. Kansas City Royals (69-93) Preseason Rank: 20

Jac Caglianone's rookie season was a nightmare, but the No. 6 overall pick in the 2024 draft looked much more the part this year, leading the Royals with both a .289 batting average and an .834 OPS. Unfortunately, this pitching staff took a colossal step backwards from last season and couldn't put Cags' breakthrough to much use.

Nos. 25-21: There Were Some Highs Amid the Many Lows

25. Cincinnati Reds (75-87) Preseason Rank: 17

Cincinnati's Big Three of Elly De La Cruz, Sal Stewart and Chase Burns was quite the triumvirate, and they're each under team control through at least 2029. The problem was, well, pretty much everyone else, as the Reds ended up bottom four in the majors in both runs scored and runs allowed in spite of those All-Star caliber players. (And, come on, how was De La Cruz not named an All-Star?)

24. Seattle Mariners (76-86) Preseason Rank: 4

Tough to put any sort of positive spin on this one. As a whole, the Mariners were the biggest disappointment in all of baseball, particularly since first place in the AL West was just there for the taking all year long. They did finally get a nice breakthrough year from Emerson Hancock, though. At least that paved the way for them to trade away Luis Castillo's contract.

23. Minnesota Twins (77-85) Preseason Rank: 25

The Twins hung around as a playoff hopeful for longer than most expected six months ago, even buying a few pitchers ahead of the trade deadline instead of repeating last year's fire sale. It turned out to be the wrong call, as they went 21-30 from August 1 onward. It was encouraging to see them actually go for it, though. And getting Pablo Lopez back from Tommy John surgery should provide quite the boost next season.

22. Washington Nationals (77-85) Preseason Rank: 30

Washington's bullpen was atrocious, blowing an MLB record 42 saves. But this offense was postseason-worthy, ranking first in steals, third in runs and sixth in home runs. And aside from the two they already traded away (Luis García Jr. and Curtis Mead), every hitter is under team control for at least two more seasons. Sign some respectable relievers this winter and they could really break through in 2027.

21. Detroit Tigers (76-86) Preseason Rank: 9

Detroit's full-season run differential (+71) was almost the same as Tampa Bay's (+86). Unfortunately, the Tigers struggled mightily in one-run games (17-27) and couldn't buy a win in May (6-22), subsequently fighting an uphill battle for months. Now, can they find the funds to bring Tarik Skubal back home?

Nos. 20-18: Two Massive Letdowns; One Pleasant Surprise

20. New York Mets (74-88) Preseason Rank: 3

Say this much for the Mets: They were much more respectable after July 4 than they were through those first few months. Good enough to lock in interim manager Andy Green on a three-year contract, at any rate.

Better yet, three of the best players on the roster were rookies. Perhaps a few of this team's extremely well-compensated veterans will pull their weight in 2027?

19. Toronto Blue Jays (79-83) Preseason Rank: 2

Toronto's entire season felt like a "one step forward, two steps backward" do-si-do, culminating in that disastrously viral quote from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. on the same day the Blue Jays got mathematically eliminated from the postseason.

Dylan Cease flirted with a Cy Young, though. Louis Varland was arguably the best reliever in the AL. And Kazuma Okamoto's four-year, $60M contract looks like an absolute steal right about now.

18. St. Louis Cardinals (77-85) Preseason Rank: 28

When the Athletics spent the 2021-22 offseason trading away every contract that they could, it was the precursor to a 102-loss season and quite the rebuild. So when the Cardinals took a similar approach this past winter—trading away Sonny Gray, Nolan Arenado, Willson Contreras and Brendan Donovan—it sure felt like they were destined for their worst season in more than a century.

Instead, they more than held their own, getting to as many as nine games above .500 on multiple occasions in the first half. Jordan Walker's breakout and JJ Wetherholt's NL ROY campaign spear-headed their surprisingly competent season.

Nos. 17-13: Should've, Would've, Could've

17. Texas Rangers (80-82) Preseason Rank: 18

The AL West was theirs for the taking all season long, but the Rangers kept refusing to seize the reins, ultimately finishing one game behind the Astros. Dropping two out of three this past week at home against the Mets was the straw that broke the camel's back, but posting losing records against both the A's and Angels this season was the real crime. It's too bad they couldn't give Jacob Latz two more leads to protect. The All-Star closer deserved a chance to pitch in the postseason.

16. Baltimore Orioles (79-82) Preseason Rank: 10

It's a shame Pete Alonso didn't really heat up until after the O's embraced a deadline fire sale, but it's hard to argue with the Polar Bear leading the AL in both home runs and RBI in his first year with the club. If Gunnar Henderson had produced like he did over the previous three seasons, that might've been enough to get Baltimore back into the playoffs.

15. Miami Marlins (80-82) Preseason Rank: 24

They sure did take a winding road to the middle of the pack, starting 26-34, winning 26 of their next 34 and going 28-40 down the stretch. During that middle section, though, we couldn't stop marveling as the Marlins came out of nowhere to almost chase down Atlanta for first place in the NL East. And for the first time since rebranding from the Florida Marlins to the Miami Marlins in 2012, they even ended up with a positive run differential (+3).

14. Pittsburgh Pirates (82-80) Preseason Rank: 21

Though they fell a few games shy of getting back to the promised land, the Pirates ended up having one of their best seasons in decades, posting a positive run differential (+28) for just the fourth time since 1993. Trading for one year of Brandon Lowe, signing Ryan O'Hearn for $29M and calling up Konnor Griffin one week into the season was an atypical combination of "We want to win now" moves from this franchise, but maybe they'll keep pulling at that thread after it did rather work out for them.

13. Arizona Diamondbacks (86-76) Preseason Rank: 22

'Twas a valiant, frantic comeback attempt by the Snakes, putting together a six-game winning streak while the Phillies suffered loss after loss at home. Unfortunately, they were in the wrong West division, eliminated from the postseason on the final day of the regular season for the second time in three years. Would have been fun to see Nolan Arenado back in the postseason after his 30-homer renaissance, but it wasn't meant to be.

Nos. 12-10: One of These Teams Will Be Playing in the ALCS

12. Houston Astros (81-81) Preseason Rank: 14

There have been a few 7-9 division winners in NFL history, and plenty of teams have made it into both the NBA and NHL postseason while finishing many games shy of .500. But for the first time in MLB history, we have a non-winning team in the playoffs.

While that's quite the unflattering distinction for these Astros, they do enter the postseason on a power surge, clubbing 32 home runs in their last 13 games to finish the regular season at No. 1 in the majors in that department.

What's more, Hunter Brown, Cristian Javier and Hayden Wesneski have each posted a sub-3.00 ERA over their last five starts.

11. Chicago White Sox (84-78) Preseason Rank: 27

A dumpster fire no more, Chicago stunned everyone by reaching the postseason after posting the worst record in the majors over the past three seasons (162-324)—including MLB's worst campaign in well over a century in 2024.

Munetaka Murakami, Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery each eclipsed 30 home runs—though the latter did set an MLB record for strikeouts in a single season (227)—as the White Sox led the American League in scoring.

However, they limped to the finish line, a sub-.500 team over their final 27 games. And though they held eight opponents to one run in September, the White Sox have what is perhaps indisputably the least intimidating pitching staff in this postseason field.

10. Cleveland Guardians (85-77) Preseason Rank: 16

Houston or Chicago could reach a World Series because weird stuff happens all the time during small sample sizes in baseball.

But Cleveland might be able to pull it off because the one-two punch of Gavin Williams and Parker Messick atop the starting rotation is no joke, while Cade Smith might be the best reliever in all of baseball. (And no, I haven't forgotten that Mason Miller exists. Smith has been that dominant for three years at this point.)

They must get José Ramírez going, though. The face of this franchise over the past decade has a .598 OPS and just two home runs since returning from his broken hamate in late July. Tough to envision Cleveland making a deep run if that continues.

9. Philadelphia Phillies (88-74) Preseason Rank: 8

After going 21-7 in August to nearly chase down Atlanta atop the NL East, the Phillies either lost or split each of their final seven series en route to a photo finish.

They held on by the skin of their teeth, though, and now hope for rejuvenated bats with their new lease on life. (Bryce Harper's homer in Game 162 might have been a spark.)

The unfortunate news is they had to burn Zack Wheeler on Sunday and won't have him (at least on normal rest) in the wild card round. Cristopher Sánchez also pitched on Friday and probably won't go until Game 2 in Atlanta. Though, cobbling together a postseason rotation certainly beats not making the postseason at all.

8. Chicago Cubs (89-73) Preseason Rank: 5

Remember when the 2023 Texas Rangers relentlessly clubbed their way to a World Series, leading the AL in regular season scoring before hitting 30 home runs in 17 games and averaging 6.5 runs per win in the postseason?

Such is Chicago's championship blueprint after leading the majors in scoring this season. At any rate, it is highly unlikely that this pitching staff (especially once the bullpens get involved) will be the driving force of a deep run.

The Cubs scored at least five runs in 85 of their games, going 71-14 when reaching that plateau. But if Pete Crow-Armstrong and Co. are held in check, they might get bounced before the calendar even flips to October.

7. San Diego Padres (91-71) Preseason Rank: 15

The San Diego Padres had a "bizarro Miami Marlins" type of season trajectory.

Instead of starting slow, catching fire for six weeks and then just kind of leaking oil for three months, San Diego went 29-18 out of the gates, dropped 35 of its next 56—Maybe gave some serious thought to trading away Mason Miller?—and had the best record in baseball (41-18) from July 24 onward.

Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill both sputtered through the first half of the season, but they've combined for 36 home runs, 23 stolen bases and a roughly .950 OPS since the All-Star Break—all while Ty France has had one of the best bounce-back seasons in recent memory.

How will the starting rotation fare in October, though?

Trading for both Robbie Ray and Casey Mize was their "all-in on 2026" sequence, but Mize is on the IL and they might leave Ray off their postseason rosters altogether. But if Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Co. can hand over leads to this loaded bullpen, best of luck taking it away.

Nos. 6-5: The Wild Cards Who Could Win It All

6. Boston Red Sox (87-75) Preseason Rank: 7

"Started from the bottom, now we're here."

When the Red Sox fired Alex Cora in late April, they had the fourth-worst record in baseball.

Two months later, they were 32-46, had just lost a series to the Colorado Rockies and would've had the worst record in the majors were it not for the 32-49 Rockies.

Since June 25, though, the Red Sox have gone an MLB-best 55-29.

Granted, that record can be broken up as 32-5 through August 7 and 23-24 since, not exactly sprinting to the finish line. But it still feels like this team is a serious threat to win it all if the offense can awake from its slumber of 89 runs scored in the past 30 games.

It's too bad they didn't fade even more down the stretch, though, as the AL's No. 6 seed has a drastically easier path to the World Series than the No. 5 seed does.

5. New York Yankees (93-68) Preseason Rank: 6

We still have no clue if Aaron Judge is going to play in Game 1 against Boston or miss the postseason altogether with his calf injury. (Frankly, you almost have to admire the gamesmanship.)

But can we stop acting like the Yankees are dead men walking if Judge doesn't play, considering they've gone 43-26 in their last 69 games while getting virtually nothing out of Judge since mid-May?

Yes, he's a three-time MVP. It's a big deal. But the actual most valuable part of this team has been the pitching staff with a 3.01 ERA dating back to July 9.

In fact, all 10 pitchers who have logged at least 26 innings during those 70 games have done so with a sub-3.60 ERA, with Cam Schlittler (1.87), Carlos Rodón (1.89) and Max Fried (2.29) really setting the tone.

Meanwhile, Ben Rice has a 1.055 OPS since the beginning of September and might be gearing up for his time in the spotlight.

Nos. 4-3: Really Good Teams Who Didn't Quite Win 100 Games

4. Atlanta Braves (94-68) Preseason Rank: 11

Traditionally, Memorial Day weekend is when you're 'allowed' to start peeking at the standings every now and then. And heading into Memorial Day weekend, these Braves looked like a juggernaut.

They were 36-16 and had already opened up a seemingly insurmountable 10.5 game lead in the NL East. They were also second in the majors in both runs scored and runs allowed per game.

Since then, they've gone 58-52 with a +11 run differential—good enough to lead the division for 170 consecutive days for what might as well have been a wire-to-wire crown, but gradually losing their early status as the team to beat in October.

Since the beginning of August—i.e. since trading for Tyler Mahle, who was the steal of the deadline—they've once again had one of the stingiest pitching staffs. However, the offense has barely even resembled its early greatness.

Can they flip the switch when it matters most? Or will it be a repeat of their last two trips to the postseason: shut out in Game 1 and immediately eliminated?

3. Tampa Bay Rays (98-64) Preseason Rank: 19

While the other four AL East teams combined to spend a little more than $887M in free agency—not to mention traded for Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Shane Baz, Ryan Weathers, Taylor Ward, Jesús Sánchez and more—the Rays became everybody's pick to finish in dead last in the division.

Little did any of us know that the Rays were going to become the MLBPA's Exhibit A in this offseason's heated arguments about a salary cap, becoming the AL's No. 1 seed for the third time in the past seven years.

Early on, it felt like smoke and mirrors. They finished April at 18-12, but with a negative run differential.

But at some point during their three-month reign atop the American League—between Victor Mesa Jr.'s breakout, Chandler Simpson's push for a batting title and giving Freddy Peralta the exact change of scenery that he evidently needed—it became clear that the Rays actually are the best team in the league as opposed to merely the AL team with the best record.

Nos. 2-1: Bring on the 2025 NLCS Rematch

2. Los Angeles Dodgers (100-62) Preseason Rank: 1

Adding Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz was supposed to be the one-two punch that enabled the free-spending Dodgers to flirt with breaking MLB's record for most wins in a single season.

Instead, they merely followed their tried-and-true blueprint from the past two World Series-winning seasons: Dominate in the first half, sputter through the doldrums of the summer and then re-ignite somewhere around Labor Day.

The Dodgers won 18 of their final 23 games, fueled in part by Tucker finally waking up for an OPS of nearly 1.000 during that closing stretch. Díaz, too, has looked like his old self since returning from his second stint on the IL and might be a major part of their postseason run after all.

Throw in the dominance of this mostly (aside from Shohei Ohtani) healthy starting rotation and Mookie Betts ending August with a .701 OPS before becoming possibly the NL Player of the Month in September and, well, here we go again.

1. Milwaukee Brewers (103-59) Preseason Rank: 1 2

One of these years, we'll learn our lesson and stop assuming that the Brewers are going to regress in a big way just because they traded away one of their best players during the offseason.

(Please print that out and smack me over the head with it if and when Milwaukee uses the final year of Willson Contreras' contract as a bartering chip this winter.)

Even as the Dodgers caught fire, the Brewers refused to give an inch in the race for home-field advantage throughout the postseason, going 18-6 with a +51 run differential in September alone.

It was their fifth consecutive month going at least five games over .500. And maybe, just maybe, this will be the year they also do so in October.

If Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser continue to shine alongside Jacob Misiorowski, you have to like their chances.

articles.title: In 1996, rookie Derek Jeter and his father started a foundation to steer young people away from drugs and alcohol; 30 years later, Turn 2 has given more than $48 million and one of its programmes has reached over 30,000 students, families and school staff
articles.summary: Long before Derek Jeter became one of baseball's biggest names, he was already thinking about what his success could mean away from the diamond.
articles.body: Long before Derek Jeter became one of baseball's biggest names, he was already thinking about what his success could mean away from the diamond. During his rookie season in 1996, Jeter and his father, Dr. Charles Jeter, created the Turn 2 Foundation with a simple goal: encourage young people to avoid drugs and alcohol while making healthier choices. Three decades later, that idea has grown into a major charitable legacy. Turn 2 says it has given back more than $48 million, while its Turn 2 Us programme alone has reached more than 30,000 students, families and school staff.Derek Jeter launched Turn 2 during his rookie seasonJeter's first full year in Major League Baseball quickly changed his life. The New York Yankees shortstop won the American League Rookie of the Year award in 1996 and helped the club win the World Series. But while his baseball career was taking off, another project was beginning outside the stadium.Jeter and his father had discussed ways to use his growing platform to help young people. That conversation eventually became the Turn 2 Foundation.The organisation was built around prevention and opportunity. Its early work focused on helping young people make positive decisions, stay away from substance abuse and develop habits that could put them on a better path. The foundation also placed a strong emphasis on education, leadership and personal development.The timing was significant. Jeter was still establishing himself as a professional athlete, yet he chose to make community work part of his identity from the beginning.That decision became a foundation of his life away from baseball.Turn 2 grew from a small idea into a major charityThe early days of Turn 2 were far less polished than the organisation is today. Jeter's first fundraising efforts were relatively modest, with an event in Kalamazoo, Michigan, raising tens of thousands of dollars.But the foundation kept growing as Jeter's career developed.Turn 2 expanded its programmes and partnerships, targeting communities where young people could benefit from extra support. Rather than focusing on one issue, the organisation developed a wider approach that included education, healthy lifestyles, leadership and career development.That broader mission helped Turn 2 remain relevant long after Jeter's playing career ended.According to the foundation's current figures, Turn 2 has now given back more than $48 million over its 30-year history. The organisation's work extends across communities in New York, Michigan and Florida, among other areas.The number is striking because Turn 2 did not begin with the resources of a major national charity. It started with a young baseball player, his father and a desire to help teenagers make better choices.Three decades later, that small beginning has become one of the most lasting parts of Jeter's legacy.Derek Jeter’s Turn 2 Us programme has reached 30,000 peopleOne of Turn 2's most notable initiatives is the Turn 2 Us programme, which demonstrates how the foundation moved from a broad mission to hands-on community work.The programme began in 2001 through a partnership involving Turn 2, NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital and Public School 128M in Washington Heights. Its focus was on helping children and the adults around them develop healthier habits and stronger support systems.The programme has since expanded to additional elementary schools.According to MLB's Turn 2 Foundation page, Turn 2 Us has served more than 30,000 students, school staff and families in Northern Manhattan and surrounding communities.That reach is important because the programme does not treat students as isolated individuals. Schools are communities, and children are influenced by teachers, parents and other adults around them.By involving students, families and school staff, Turn 2 Us creates a wider network of support.The programme also reflects the foundation's original philosophy. Prevention is not simply about telling young people what not to do. It is about giving them useful alternatives, trusted adults and opportunities to build confidence.For a foundation that began with a goal of steering young people away from drugs and alcohol, that approach has allowed the mission to evolve without losing its original purpose.Derek Jeter’s legacy extends beyond his Yankees careerJeter's baseball résumé is already enough to secure his place in sports history. He spent his entire 20-year MLB career with the Yankees, collected five World Series titles and finished with more than 3,400 hits. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2020.Yet Turn 2 represents a different kind of record.There is no batting average attached to a foundation. No championship ring measures the effect of helping a teenager develop healthier habits or giving a family access to support. The impact can be harder to see, but it can last much longer.That is particularly clear when looking at how Turn 2 has developed over 30 years.Jeter's transition from a rookie baseball player to a retired superstar did not end his connection with the organisation. Instead, Turn 2 continued building programmes around the same themes that inspired its creation.The foundation now focuses on helping young people pursue education, healthy lifestyles and leadership opportunities. It also supports programmes designed to strengthen families and communities.The $48 million figure tells only part of the story. The more personal measure may be the number of people who encountered Turn 2 through a school, community programme or educational initiative.For Jeter, the project began at a moment when his own future was still uncertain. He was a rookie trying to establish himself in the majors. Thirty years later, his baseball career is over, but the organisation he started with his father continues to work with young people.That may be the most meaningful part of the Turn 2 story.Jeter entered the Yankees clubhouse as a promising 22-year-old and eventually became one of baseball's most recognisable figures. But while the statistics tell the story of his career on the field, Turn 2 offers another set of numbers: more than $48 million given back and more than 30,000 people reached through Turn 2 Us.The foundation's story shows how a decision made during a rookie season can outlast a playing career by decades. The New York Mets may have fallen massively short of expectations in 2026, but at least they have a chance to replenish their farm system in next year's draft.

The Colorado Rockies, Los Angeles Angels and Athletics are the three teams at the top of the lottery odds. They have a 19.1 percent chance of landing the No. 1 overall pick and are 87.6 percent on for staying in the top six.

The Mets are long shots for the first pick but should at least hang around the top six:

The 2026 draft opened with a pair of shortstops: UCLA's Roch Cholowsky and prep prospect Grady Emerson. Next year could be a similar story.

In his early projections for 2027, MLB.com's Jonathan Mayo led off with high schooler Dylan Seward and Florida star Brendan Lawson. Joel Reuter of Bleacher Report mocked Seward at No. 2 behind Mississippi State pitcher Tomas Valincius. Lawson went fourth overall.

Reuter called Seward "a quick-twitch athlete with top-of-the-scale speed, advanced bat-to-ball skills and elite bat speed to generate some playable power even with a 6'0", 175-pound frame."

Whoever lands the No. 1 pick may prefer a more polished prospect, much as the White Sox did with Cholowsky.

Lawson had a .511 on-base percentage and slugged .699 with the Gators in 2026. His homer total nearly doubled, going from 10 as a freshman to 19.

Valincius, who transferred to the Bulldogs from Virginia, went 11-2 with a 3.50 ERA in 17 starts. He struck out 134 batters in 97.2 innings. More of the same in 2027 will make him the best pitcher in the class.

articles.title: Explaining MLB Playoff Bracket 2026 Wild Card Format, Divisional Series and More
articles.summary: The 2026 Major League Baseball postseason gets underway Tuesday with four wild-card series.
articles.body:
The 2026 Major League Baseball postseason gets underway Tuesday with four wild-card series.

The wild-card round produced mixed results over the last two years. In 2024, three of the four best-of-three series were over in two games. A year ago, three of the four series went the distance.

Two divisional rivalries headline the 2026 wild-card round. The New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox do battle in the American League, while the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies square off in the National League.

History is not on the side of the wild-card teams, though, as only one wild-card participant qualified for the World Series in the last two seasons.

The Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians all get almost a week of rest before they start the postseason in the divisional round.

The wild-card round is a best-of-three format held exclusively at the home ball parks of the Nos. 3 and 4 seeds.

Atlanta faces Philadelphia in the marquee NL series. The San Diego Padres host the Chicago Cubs in the other NL matchup.

The Yankees-Red Sox series headlines the AL wild-card round. The Houston Astros host the Chicago White Sox in the other matchup.

The four wild-card winners will advance to the divisional round to play the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds in best-of-five series.

The two ALDS and NLDS winners will then meet in the best-of-seven ALCS and NLCS. The pennant winners in each league square off in the 2026 World Series.

The divisional round starts on October 3. The NLCS begins on October 11, with the ALCS starting one day later on October 12. The World Series is slated to start on October 23.

Game 3: Thursday, 2 p.m. ET, NBC (if necessary)

No. 6 Chicago White Sox at No. 3 Houston

Game 1: Tuesday, 5 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN

Game 2: Wednesday, 5 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN

Game 3: Thursday, 5 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN (if necessary)

Game 3: Thursday, 8 p.m. ET, NBC (if necessary)

Game 1: Tuesday, 10 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN

Game 2: Wednesday, 10 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN

Game 3: Thursday, 10 p.m. ET, Peacock/NBCSN (if necessary)

Houston carries far more postseason experience than the Chicago White Sox, who were not expected to make the playoffs with their young core.

The Astros won the season series 5-2, but they enter the postseason with the worst staff ERA at 4.45.

Houston did hit the most home runs in the majors, led by Yordan Alvarez, and that might be the way it has to win games in the postseason.

The AL West champion can't win series with dominant pitching, like it did in previous season, so it will be fascinating to see which hurlers rise to the occasion in 2026.

The White Sox lineup had the most strikeouts of any playoff team. That's a big concern to go along with the inexperience strewn across their rotation.

However, the White Sox did go 6-2 in their last eight games and scored 54 runs in the process. There's a chance they can carry over that hot hitting into the postseason and spring an upset.

The Yankees rotation is built for the postseason.

Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole will pitch in that order against the Red Sox.

Schlittler allowed one earned run in three starts against the Red Sox in the regular season. Fried let up one run in 11.2 innings versus Boston. Cole had the worst outing of the three against Boston on June 27 with five earned runs, but there's a chance the Red Sox don't even get a chance to hit off him.

Boston can counter with Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle, but they need to be near perfect in Games 1 and 2 for the Red Sox to have a shot at Cole.

Tolle struck out 18 Yankees in two starts against them in 2026, while Gray allowed three earned runs over 13.2 innings versus the Yankees.

A low-scoring series seems to be in the cards, especially with Aaron Judge on the injured list for the Yankees.

A handful of tight, one-run games are expected given how strong all the projected starters performed in the rivalry during the regular season.

The Phillies went 2-6 in their final eight games and needed a win in Game 162 just to qualify for the postseason.

The wild-card team had to use ace Zack Wheeler on Sunday to confirm its postseason spot, so that takes him out of the first two games as a potential starter.

Cristopher Sanchez will pitch one of the first two games in Atlanta, but the rest of the rotation is a mystery because Jesus Luzardo just came off the injured list.

Atlanta will run with Chris Sale in Game 1 and then hope its makeshift rotation can get it into the NLDS. Tyler Mahle and Grant Holmes are the most likely starters behind Sale in an injury-riddled rotation.

The Braves went 4-3 in September against the Phillies, including a 2-1 record at home in a series that essentially clinched the NL East for them.

The NL East champion has the more consistent lineup, but the Phillies have the higher quality starting pitching. That might be enough for the No. 6 seed to spring an upset.

Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Chicago Cubs struggled to score for most of the final week of the regular season. They scored more than two runs in a game twice during a 2-4 week in which they were overtaken by San Diego for the No. 4 seed.

The Cubs won five of their six regular-season games with the Padres, but all of those games were played before the All-Star break.

San Diego was one of the best MLB teams in September. It washed away most of its first-half struggles and looks like a formidable force in the NL bracket.

The Padres probably have a little revenge on their minds, too, after they lost in the wild-card round at Wrigley Field a year ago.

It's hard to deny how well the Padres played down the stretch, and if that continues into the postseason, they might be able to make a deep run in the NL.

articles.title: Latest Expert MLB Playoff Predictions and Picks for 2026 World Series Bracket
articles.summary: The 12-team fight to MLB's finish line and the World Series trophy that comes along with it starts now.
articles.body:
The 12-team fight to MLB's finish line and the World Series trophy that comes along with it starts now.

OK, maybe not now now, but with the regular season closed and the playoff field set, these franchsies know exactly what stands between them and championship glory.

While no one knows which organization will rise above and how the other 11 will get tripped up, multiple experts have shared their ideas. Let's break down some of those expert picks to get a feel for what might be coming to an MLB playoff environment near you.

Between Yahoo Sports and CBS Sports , there are full round-by-round predictions from nine different experts. Among the four Wild-Card Round matchups, there isn't universal agreement on any of them.

There is, however, one series that comes awfully close. Eight of the nine experts have the New York Yankees knocking off their longtime rival Boston Red Sox.

No other series had more than six experts agreeing on one side. The closest were the Atlanta Braves beating the Philadelphia Phillies, and the San Diego Padres ousting the Chicago Cubs, which both outcomes appearing on six of nine brackets. The biggest split came between the Chicago White Sox and Houston Astros with five favoring the former and four backing the latter.

Advancing a round didn't bring our first universal agreement among the experts. One came awfully close, though. ( And, yes, it is exactly what you're thinking .)

The two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers were projected Division Series winners by eight of the nine experts. The only dissenter, CBS Sports' Dayn Perry, backed the Braves.

Experts saw two other heavy favorites in the field. Both the Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers were picked by seven of the nine experts. The Yankees snagged the other two picks on the AL side, while the Cubs and Padres drew one apiece in the NL.

The only team with a first-round bye that didn't receive overwhelming support was the Cleveland Guardians, which checks out when they were the only non-98-plus-game winner among the top two seeds (they won 85). Cleveland was predicted to escape this round by five experts, while four went with the resurgent White Sox, who followed three consecutive 100-loss seasons with an 84-win rise.

The closer these projections get to the finish line, the more the opinions split.

In the AL, the consensus opinion among the experts crowned the Rays, who drew six of the nine votes. That included four picks of them over the Guardians and two where they knocked off the White Sox. For the other outcomes, two had the Yankees defeating the Guardians, while one went Cleveland over Tampa Bay.

In the NL, it was the Brewers—not the Dodgers—receiving the most love. Six different experts had Milwaukee escaping the NL: three by beating L.A., two by eliminating San Diego and one by knocking off the Cubs. The Dodgers, meanwhile, were twice predicted NL winners (once over the Brewers, once over the Padres), while the Padres were the last predicted winner (over the Dodgers).

Now that we've made it this far, let's crown some (predicted) World Series champions, shall we?

The Brewers received the strongest backing with five of the nine experts going their way. The most popular World Series pick was Milwaukee over Tampa (four experts' opinons), while one more had Milwaukee defeating New York.

The Rays and Dodgers were the only other predicted winners, as they split the final four votes. Tampa's predicted wins came over San Diego and L.A., while L.A.'s were against Cleveland and New York.

articles.title: MLB Average Game Times Increased Following Robot Umpires and ABS Challenge System
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's use of the Automated Ball-Strike Challenge System this season has been met with significant praise, but it also made the games longer.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball's use of the Automated Ball-Strike Challenge System this season has been met with significant praise , but it also made the games longer.

The Associated Press reported Monday the average time of a nine-inning game this season was two hours and 42 minutes, which is three minutes and 43 seconds longer than it was last year without the ABS system and strike-ball challenges in place.

The AP noted MLB said 61 seconds of this season's increase was because of ABS, although the average game length is still well down from 2022 when it was three hours and four minutes.

MLB instituted the pitch clock after that 2022 campaign, which has consistently meant games lasting fewer than three hours.

And that was once again the case this season even though there was a slight increase.
